title: THE LONG WAY UP · GET-UPS, REPEATS & CRAWLS
vibe: GREEN · 7 hours of good sleep, nothing sore, a full rest day in the bank, and you want to go hard. So today goes to the floor. Two blocks are governed by your BREATH, not a clock — if you have to open your mouth, you rest. One block in the middle is where you empty the tank. Nothing today is counted the way anything was counted this week.
why: Three things built today. First, the hole. Go down the coverage list — squat, hinge, push, pull, carry, core, GET-UP, run — and the get-up is the only pattern that has never once led a session. It has shown up as a station in a gauntlet, as a half rep in a core block, never as the thing itself. Today it is the thing itself: ten unbroken minutes, forty pounds, one rep a side, and the only rule is that you keep breathing through your nose. That single rule turns a skill drill into a grind, because a get-up at 250 pounds will absolutely make you want to gasp, and you are not allowed to. Second, the run. On Tuesday you took a prescribed 1.5-mile speed ladder and ran three continuous miles instead — 7:36, 7:33, 7:22, descending the whole way, and you called it really good. That is the second time in a week you have voluntarily added distance when pace was not the target, so consider the duration lever proven and put away. Today goes the exact opposite direction: two miles total instead of three, both of them faster than anything you have sustained for a mile in this log, with a float in between. Mile repeats. First ones on your plan, and the obvious workout to give a man who ran collegiately and never got them. Third, the way effort gets measured. Look at this week — Saturday counted pounds and rest, Tuesday counted rungs and quarter-miles. Today counts breath and it counts ground covered. You will finish the session crawling backwards across your own floor under nothing but your bodyweight, and that will be the part that surprises you. The jerk question from Tuesday is still open and I am deliberately parking it — it needs a fresh session with fresh shoulders, not a footnote after two hard miles.

blocks.title: MOBILITY WARM-UP · THE FLOW
blocks.meta: ~6 min · Moves Method Day C · rotated off Day A on Tuesday and Day B on Saturday · everything today happens on the ground, so warm up on the ground
blocks.text: No stations, no counting, no stopping. This is one continuous moving sequence and it is the same vocabulary the session is written in — you are rehearsing the finisher, not preparing for it. Start on your back: segmental rolls, roll from your back to your stomach leading with one arm only, no momentum, 3 each direction · dead bug cross-crawls, opposite hand to opposite knee, 20 slow taps · then roll to all fours. Rock backs, sit your hips toward your heels and come forward, 15 of them, and let your head lead the movement · cross-crawls on all fours, reaching one hand and the opposite knee off the floor, 20 total · then take the knees off the floor into a bear-crawl hold and just breathe there for 20 seconds, hips low, back flat enough to balance a glass on. Then crawl forward 3 lengths of whatever floor you have and backward 3 lengths. Finish standing: 10 arm circles each direction, then 10 slow bodyweight get-up sit-ups (no bell, just come from flat on your back up to the elbow and back down) so the first loaded rep is not the first rep of the day.

blocks.title: BLOCK 1 · NON-STOP GET-UPS
blocks.meta: 10 min continuous · 40 lb · alternate one rep per side · NASAL BREATHING IS THE GOVERNOR · count total reps
blocks.format: CONTINUOUS DENSITY · no sets, no rest intervals, no rep target on the clock · the only stop signal is your breath
blocks.workRest: Set the countdown for 10 minutes and go. One get-up left, one get-up right, back to left, and keep going for the full ten. There is no prescribed rest — you rest exactly as much as you need to KEEP BREATHING THROUGH YOUR NOSE, and not one second more. The moment your mouth opens, you have gone too fast: put the bell down, stand there, get your nose back, pick it up and continue. That is the whole method. GREEN target is 12 total reps (6 per side). YELLOW is 8. A get-up is not a rep you rush — every one of these should look like the first one.

items.name: TURKISH GET-UP · alternating 1 rep per side, 10 min
items.detail: 40 lb. Full formal get-up, floor to standing and back to the floor, every step: roll to press, punch the bell up, post on your elbow, up to your hand, sweep the leg through, hips high, knee down, windshield-wiper to a lunge, stand. Then reverse all of it. Eyes on the bell the whole way up and the whole way down. This is the strength load, not the skill load — 40 pounds should feel meaningful overhead by rep 8, and your shoulder should be doing real work holding it in the socket. Slow is the point. The clock is not a target, it is a container.

items.name: THE BREATH RULE (this is the training effect)
items.detail: Nose in, nose out, the entire ten minutes, including while you are moving under the bell. This is the Original Strength governor and it is the first time this program has measured effort with anything other than a clock, a rep count, or a speed. It does three things at once: it caps your pace so the reps stay clean, it forces your diaphragm to work while your midline is loaded overhead, and it tells you exactly when you are actually recovered instead of guessing. Ten minutes of this at 40 pounds is deceptively hard. If you get to minute seven and you are still nasal-breathing comfortably, that is when you speed up the transitions.

items.name: THE QUESTION FOR TODAY
items.detail: Which step of the get-up is the one where your breath breaks? For most people it is the hip bridge or the moment you sweep the leg through. Whichever step makes you want to open your mouth is the step that is costing you the most, and that is what I want reported back — that plus your total rep count.

blocks.text: The get-up is the one movement pattern in the coverage list that has never headlined a day in this program. It has been a station inside the BIG 6 gauntlet on the 1st and a half rep in a core block on the 27th, and that is it. It is also the single best answer to the thing your log keeps circling: shoulder stability under load, midline control, and grip — grip being what failed you first in the Olympic chain, not lungs. Ten minutes of loaded get-ups charges all three, and it costs your legs nothing, which matters because your legs have two hard miles coming.

blocks.title: BLOCK 2 · MILE REPEATS
blocks.meta: ~17 min · treadmill · 0% incline · 2 × 1 mile with a float · THIS is where the session gets hard · breathe however you need to
blocks.format: MILE REPEATS · 2 × 1 mile, negative split, 2-min float between · the first mile repeats in this log
blocks.workRest: Two miles of work, one float. Forget nasal breathing here — that rule belongs to the blocks on either side of this one. This block is the opposite: you are supposed to be breathing hard and you are supposed to want the float. Watch the DISTANCE readout for the miles and the clock only for the float. Cadence 168 to 172, short quick steps, especially on the second one when you get tired and start reaching. Both repeats are faster than any sustained mile in your log — Tuesday's fastest mile was the third of three at 7:22, so mile one today starts just past that and mile two goes somewhere you have not been.

items.name: REPEAT 1 · 1.0 mi @ 7.9 console
items.detail: Target split ~7:15 on your watch. Set it and settle — do not go out over the top for the first quarter, this is the controlled one. It should feel like a hard tempo, not a race: breathing heavy, form intact, and you should finish it thinking you could have gone faster. That thought is correct and it is the entire setup for repeat two.

items.name: FLOAT · 2:00 @ 6.0 console
items.detail: Two minutes, keep running, do not walk and do not step off the belt. A float is not a rest — it is the part of a repeat workout that actually builds the engine, because you are asking your heart rate to come down while your legs are still turning over. Get your breathing organized on a rhythm. When the two minutes are up you go straight into the second mile with no pause.

items.name: REPEAT 2 · 1.0 mi @ 8.1 console
items.detail: Target split ~7:05 on your watch. Faster than the first, off a float instead of off fresh legs. This is a negative split under fatigue, which is the harder version of the thing you already do naturally in every run in this log. Stay tall through the third quarter when it starts to bite. THE HOOK: if you come through the 3/4 mark still in control, bump the belt to 8.3 and finish the last quarter there. That call is yours to make in the moment and I want to know whether you took it.

items.name: WALK DOWN · 90 sec @ 3.0
items.detail: Stay on the belt and walk it out for a full minute and a half before you go back to the floor. You have a crawling block next and going straight from 8.1 to hands-and-knees with your heart rate still at the ceiling will make the finisher worse than it needs to be. Use the ninety seconds.

blocks.text: Every run you have been given lately has been counted in minutes or in fractions of a mile: a fartlek on the 28th, an 18-minute aerobic block on the 1st that you stretched to 21, a climb on the 2nd, a descending distance ladder on the 5th that you ignored in favor of running three straight miles. So distance is proven and duration is proven. What has never been on your plan is the oldest workout in distance running — repeat the same distance twice, faster than you would race it in a continuous run, with a float between. You ran collegiately; you have done hundreds of these. This program had never given you one.

blocks.title: BLOCK 3 · THE CRAWL & CARRY GAUNTLET
blocks.meta: 10 min · bodyweight + 2×40 lb + 50 lb DB · measured in LENGTHS OF FLOOR, not reps · nasal breathing is back on · this is the core block
blocks.format: LOADED LOCOMOTION · 4-station cycle, repeat continuously for 10 min · count total lengths
blocks.workRest: One length equals whatever your longest clear run of floor is — call it 10 to 20 steps and use the same distance every time so the count means something. Cycle the four stations in order and keep repeating for ten minutes. NASAL BREATHING IS BACK ON: rest between lengths as much as you need to keep your mouth shut, but keep the feet moving when you can. This is your dedicated core block for the day and it does not look like one, which is the point — crawling is anti-rotation with your whole body, and a loaded carry is anti-lateral-flexion you cannot cheat. Rotating off the last four core blocks: renegade rows and dead bugs on Tuesday, a carry ladder on Saturday, figure-8s and hollow holds on the 1st, chops and lateral walks on the 28th. GREEN target is 8 total lengths (2 full cycles). YELLOW is 4.

items.name: 1 · BACKWARD LEOPARD CRAWL · 1 length (WILDCARD)
items.detail: Bodyweight. NEW — has never been in your log in either direction, and backward is the harder one by a wide margin. Hands and toes, knees hovering an inch off the floor, hips low, and you travel FEET FIRST. Opposite hand and opposite foot move together, same as crawling forward, just reversed. Your knees never touch down. At 250 pounds this is a full-body isometric that happens to move, and going backward loads your triceps and shoulders in a way nothing else in this program does. Walk back to the start.

items.name: 2 · FARMER CARRY · 1 length down and back
items.detail: 2×40 lb, 80 pounds total — about 32% of your bodyweight, right in the band Original Strength programs carries at. Bells hanging at your sides, shoulders packed down and back, ribs down, walk tall and quick. Do not lean. Grip is the currency you are always short on and this is the direct deposit. Set them down at the far end, turn around, pick them up, walk back.

items.name: 3 · CRAB CRAWL · 1 length (WILDCARD)
items.detail: Bodyweight, and also new. Sit down, hands behind you with fingers pointing toward your feet, feet flat, lift your hips so you are a table facing the ceiling, and travel. Keep the hips UP the entire length — the second they sag, the exercise stops working. This is the direct counter to everything else in the session: ten minutes of get-ups and two miles of running both put you in flexion, and this is the only thing on the plan that drives your chest open and your hips forward under load. It is also, per the people who program it, brutal. Expect your wrists and shoulders to complain and go anyway.

items.name: 4 · SUITCASE CARRY · 1 length each hand
items.detail: 50 lb DB, one hand. Down in the right, back in the left. Walk like nothing is in your hand — level shoulders, no lean toward the weight, no hitch in the hip. Every step is a rep of not bending sideways, and this is the piece that most directly protects the low back that keeps showing up stiff in your check-ins. Then straight back to station 1 and go again.

blocks.text: Tim Anderson's rule for this is 'pick one, then carry or crawl' — get-ups on their own, then ten minutes of ground work, all of it under nasal breathing. That is the whole shape of today. The reason it belongs at the end rather than the start is that crawling under fatigue is where it actually teaches you something: your shoulders are cooked from get-ups, your legs are cooked from two hard miles, and you are going to find out that moving your own bodyweight across a floor is not the easy part of the session.

blocks.title: COOLDOWN
blocks.meta: ~4 min · wrists and shoulders from the crawling, hip flexors from the get-ups, calves from the repeats
blocks.text: Wrist flexor and extensor stretch, 30s each direction — palms down on the floor then flip them over, you just spent ten minutes on your hands · child's pose with the hands walked out and to each side, 45s per side, to open the lats after all that overhead work · couch stretch or a half-kneeling hip flexor stretch, 45s per side — get-ups load the hip flexor hard on every sweep-through · calf stretch against a wall, 45s per side, straight knee then bent knee, after two miles at 7:15 and 7:05 · finish flat on your back with your legs up the wall for 60 seconds, and breathe through your nose one more time, slow, until your heart rate is genuinely down. Report back: total get-ups, which step broke your breath, both mile splits off the watch, whether you took the 8.3 at the end, and how many lengths of the gauntlet you got.

timer.emomUnit: No EMOM today. Use the COUNTDOWN twice, both set to 10 minutes: once for Non-Stop Get-Ups and once for the Crawl & Carry Gauntlet. The mile repeats run off the treadmill's DISTANCE readout — the only clock in that block is the 2-minute float and the 90-second walk down. Nothing in this session is measured in reps on a minute.
